q: You charter a yacht with a fixed VHF. Which document covers the radio set itself?
a: The ship station radio licence
o: Your VHF operator's certificate
The charter contract
The boat's insurance policy
why: The ship station licence covers the boat's radio equipment; the certificate covers the operator.

q: You read through your boat's ship station licence. What does it list?
a: The boat's call sign, MMSI and radio equipment
o: The skipper's name and qualification
The crew list with passport numbers
The cruising area and the season dates
why: The ship station licence names the vessel, its call sign, MMSI and licensed equipment.

q: You sell your yacht and buy a different one. What happens to your VHF operator's certificate?
a: It stays with you — it is personal
o: It passes to the buyer with the boat
It must be reissued for the new boat
It lapses when the old boat is sold
why: The operator's certificate belongs to the person; the station licence belongs to the boat.

q: Your crew want to use the VHF to chat with friends on another yacht. Whose decision is it?
a: The skipper's — the radio is under their authority
o: Anyone's who holds a radio certificate
The owner's, even when not aboard
The coastguard's, by permission on air
why: The ship's radio station is under the authority of the master or skipper.

q: On a working channel you overhear two yachts discussing a private family matter. May you tell others what you heard?
a: No — overheard traffic must stay secret
o: Yes — it was on an open channel
Yes, but only to your own crew
Yes, once their conversation has ended
why: Secrecy of correspondence: you may not pass on what you overhear (distress traffic aside).

q: You noted down a MAYDAY that the coast station seems not to have heard. May you pass its details on to the coastguard?
a: Yes — distress traffic is the exception
o: No — secrecy covers all radio traffic
Only with the casualty's permission
Only after SEELONCE FEENEE is given
why: Secrecy never stops you passing on distress traffic.

q: Your guest is about to press the transmit key. What do you tell him?
a: No — a false distress call is prohibited
o: Fine, as long as he uses low power
Fine, if he says "test" afterwards
Fine on a working channel, not 16
why: False or deceptive distress signals are forbidden and may launch a real rescue.

fig.title: On deck
lines: A teenage guest picks up the mic
Wants to say MAYDAY "as a test"

q: Which of these transmissions breaks the radio rules?
a: Calling the marina without giving your boat's name
o: A short radio check with the marina
Calling the marina on its working channel
A SÉCURITÉ about a drifting container
why: Every transmission must identify the station; transmissions without identification are prohibited.

q: Bored on night watch, a crew member keeps clicking the transmit key on 16 to "say hello" to a friend's boat. What is wrong?
a: Unnecessary signals are prohibited
o: Nothing, if the clicks are short
Nothing, since it is done at night
Nothing, if the set is on low power
why: Unnecessary transmissions and signals are prohibited — and they can mask a weak distress call.

q: Several calls are waiting for a quiet channel. In which order of priority do they go?
a: Distress, urgency, safety, routine
o: Urgency, distress, safety, routine
Distress, safety, urgency, routine
Safety, distress, urgency, routine
why: Priority: distress (MAYDAY), urgency (PAN-PAN), safety (SÉCURITÉ), then routine.

q: Which radio traffic should you note in your log, like these entries?
a: Distress, urgency and safety traffic sent or heard
o: Every routine call you make all day
Only the calls that coast stations make
Nothing — logs are only for big ships
why: Record distress, urgency and safety traffic heard or sent, with times — it may be needed later.

q: You sail your own yacht, licensed in your home country, into Greek waters. Can you use her VHF there?
a: Yes, under her licence and the local rules
o: No — she needs a Greek ship licence first
Only on channel 16, for nothing else
Only after registering at each port
why: A ship station licence is valid internationally; in foreign waters you also follow local regulations.

q: Your crew member has no radio certificate. You hold one and stand beside her. May she call the marina?
a: Yes — under your supervision
o: No — only you may touch the set
Yes, but only on low power
Only calls to a coast station
why: Someone without a certificate may operate the radio under the supervision of a certificate holder.

q: May Anna make the routine call to the marina herself?
a: Not alone — she must wait for you
o: Yes — routine calls need no certificate
Yes, if she gives your certificate number
Yes, if she keeps the set on low power
why: Without a certificate she may only operate under a holder's supervision (distress excepted).

fig.title: Afternoon at anchor
lines: Anna wants to book a berth by VHF

q: Your crew member is losing his temper on the radio. What do you do?
a: Stop him — obscene language is prohibited
o: Let him — it is only a working channel
Let him, as long as he gives the boat name
Let him finish, then apologise yourself
why: Obscene or abusive language on the radio is prohibited.

fig.title: Berth dispute
lines: Another skipper took your booked berth
Your crew grabs the VHF, furious
Starts swearing at him on air

q: Three messages are waiting to go out. In which order should they be sent?
a: A, B, C
o: B, A, C
C, A, B
A, C, B
why: Urgency (drifting without engine, PAN-PAN) before safety (the buoy, SÉCURITÉ) before routine.

fig.title: Waiting to transmit
lines: A: engine dead, drifting, tow needed
B: warning of an unlit buoy

q: Ashore at a taverna, you want to call your crew on the boat with the yacht's handheld marine VHF. Is that allowed?
a: No — marine VHF is not for use from land
o: Yes, on low power only
Yes, on channel 16 only
Yes, within a mile of the boat
why: Marine VHF is licensed for the maritime service; using it from land generally needs special permission.

q: With these papers aboard, may you use the charter yacht's VHF?
a: Yes — her licence and your certificate cover it
o: No — the licence must be in your own name
Only on channel 16, and only in distress
Only once the firm informs the coastguard
why: The boat's station licence covers the set; your certificate covers you as the operator.

fig.title: Charter yacht
lines: Ship licence: in the charter firm's name

q: A port official inspecting your yacht asks for her radio documents. What do you show?
a: Ship station licence and operator's certificate
o: Only your passport and the crew list
The VHF's manual and its receipt
The charter contract and insurance
why: Keep the station licence and the operator's certificate aboard, ready for inspection.

q: A friend suggests you use his boat's name on your radio so that your own boat stays "off the air". What do you say?
a: No — false identification is prohibited
o: Fine, if his boat is not at sea today
Fine, as long as you use low power
Fine, but only on working channels
why: You must identify your own station correctly; false identification is prohibited.
